article_title: Researching Digital Learning Platforms: Foundations, Methods, and Policy Recommendations
citation: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257
title: DLP-as-research-infrastructure: platforms as dynamic environments that shape, capture, and reflect learning
description: The paper's central organizing framework is that digital learning platforms are more than delivery mechanisms: they are evolving into research infrastructure. Whereas most edtech research treats platforms as external interventions, the authors argue platforms provide interaction data—clickstreams, hint requests, response sequences—that can support theory-connected inquiry. As they put it, DLPs are 'evolving into research infrastructures capable of supporting systematic inquiry into learning, design, and fairness at scale.'
requirements: Platforms must provide detailed interaction data such as clickstreams, time-on-task, hint requests, and response sequences, and must permit researcher access and transparency
constraints: Most commercial or institutionally adopted platforms offer limited or inconsistent access to backend data, which restricts reproducibility and secondary analysis
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students using digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Understanding learning processes, instructional design effectiveness, and fairness in digital learning environments
examples: ASSISTments, Google Classroom, Khan Academy, MATHia, Moodle, and other platforms are described as providing structured environments plus detailed interaction data used to study engagement, scaffolds, and adaptive feedback
key_sources: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257

article_title: Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning
citation: Tatyana Ivanova. (2026). Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning. Mathematics 2026, 14, 808. https://doi.org/10.3390/math14050808
title: Manage DL reasoning complexity through OWL profile targets, TBox/ABox separation, and layered ontology decomposition
description: The article identifies balancing expressiveness and computational complexity as a core design decision in DL ontologies and lists design principles for decreasing reasoning complexity: using OWL Profiles as design targets, separating TBox and ABox reasoning and pushing complex logic into rules where possible, and decomposing ontologies into layers, using EL for large core taxonomies and OWL DL for smaller logically complex sub-ontologies. The article states that "Balancing expressiveness and computational complexity is one of the core design decisions in DL ontologies."
requirements: Evaluation of DL reasoners against specific requirements before selecting a reasoner for a particular application
constraints: The article advises avoiding OWL Full if possible, since it is undecidable
target_learners: developers of educational ontologies and knowledge-based intelligent educational systems
target_learning_goals: efficient reasoning support for personalization in knowledge-based e-learning systems
examples: Table 4 lists well-working DL reasoners (FaCT++, HermiT, ELK, Ontop, Pellet) with their algorithms and complexity classes
key_sources: Tatyana Ivanova. (2026). Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning. Mathematics 2026, 14, 808. https://doi.org/10.3390/math14050808

article_title: A Longitudinal Examination of Racial Identity and Racial Discrimination Among African American Adolescents
citation: Seaton Eleanor K., Yip Tiffany, Sellers Robert M. (2009). A Longitudinal Examination of Racial Identity and Racial Discrimination Among African American Adolescents. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2009.01268.x
title: Daily Life Experiences (DLE) scale for adolescent perceived racial discrimination frequency
description: The DLE is a self-report subscale of the Racism and Life Experiences Scale assessing "daily hassles or the frequency of 'microaggressions' because of race in the past year". Participants rated 18 discriminatory experiences (e.g., "Having your ideas ignored", "Not being taken seriously") on a 0–5 frequency scale. In this sample internal consistency was high at all waves (T1 α = .93; T2 α = .92; T3 α = .92), and the mean across items was computed at each time point.
requirements: Annual recall period; the authors note smaller time periods or experiential sampling might capture discriminatory experiences more precisely
constraints: The authors note daily diary research has found discrimination to be a low frequency event, so measurement warrants further attention
target_learners: African American adolescents in grades spanning middle and high school
target_learning_goals: Measuring frequency of everyday racial discrimination experiences in longitudinal research
examples: Used at three annual waves with the 219-adolescent sample in the present study
key_sources: Seaton Eleanor K., Yip Tiffany, Sellers Robert M. (2009). A Longitudinal Examination of Racial Identity and Racial Discrimination Among African American Adolescents. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2009.01268.x

article_title: Exploring the structure of digital literacy competence assessed using authentic software applications
citation: Frank Reichert, Nancy W. Y. Law, Gary K. W. Wong, Jimmy de la Torre. (2020). Exploring the structure of digital literacy competence assessed with authentic software applications. Education Tech Research Dev, 68, 2991–3013. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09825-x
title: Bifactor model of digital literacy competence: a general DL dimension supplemented by tool-specific dimensions
description: The article proposes that DL as assessed through authentic software is best modeled as a hierarchical bifactor structure: a general dimension measured by all items representing the "essence" of DL, plus specific residual dimensions capturing commonality not accounted for by the general dimension. In the ILPA data these specific dimensions were defined by the software applications used (online information seeking, knowledge-based information seeking, word processing, digital presentation), challenging frameworks that depict DL as a generic, tool-independent competence.
requirements: Assessment data collected with authentic software applications and items detailed enough for multidimensional IRT modeling
constraints: The specific dimensions do not map well onto existing DL frameworks; the structure was established on 2007 ILPA data from Hong Kong using Microsoft Office applications
examples: The bifactor model fit the ILPA data better (RMSEA = .052, CFI = .978) than a four-dimensional model without a general dimension
key_sources: Frank Reichert, Nancy W. Y. Law, Gary K. W. Wong, Jimmy de la Torre. (2020). Exploring the structure of digital literacy competence assessed with authentic software applications. Education Tech Research Dev, 68, 2991–3013. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09825-x

article_title: Digital Learning to Improve Safe and Effective Prescribing: A Systematic Review.
citation: Bakkum, M.J., Tichelaar, J., Wellink, A., Richir, M.C. & van Agtmael, M.A. (2019). Digital Learning to Improve Safe and Effective Prescribing: A Systematic Review. Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics. https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.1549
title: Taxonomy of digital learning resource types for prescribing education
description: The review classifies digital learning resources into defined types used to categorize interventions: e-learning, digital assessment, social component, podcasts, blended learning, virtual patient, virtual reality, augmented reality, and serious/educational games. E-learning is defined as a "Web‐based (online) or offline course offering a mixture of text, multimedia, and interactive elements," and blended learning as any DLR combined with face-to-face teaching. The taxonomy structures the review's analysis of which DLR types are used and how effective they are, with e-learning the most-used type (55 of 65 articles).
requirements: Articles must describe or evaluate at least one DLR for teaching safe and effective prescribing to graduate or undergraduate prescribers
constraints: Definitions were adapted from prior work (van den Berg et al. and Piovesan et al.) and applied with reviewer consensus decisions, limiting repeatability
examples: The review categorized 55 articles as e-learning, 12 as blended learning, 6 as digital assessment, and 9 as unique interventions such as gamified e-learning, a text-based virtual patient, and informative podcasts
key_sources: Bakkum, M.J., Tichelaar, J., Wellink, A., Richir, M.C. & van Agtmael, M.A. (2019). Digital Learning to Improve Safe and Effective Prescribing: A Systematic Review. Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics. https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.1549

article_title: Digital Learning to Improve Safe and Effective Prescribing: A Systematic Review.
citation: Bakkum, M.J., Tichelaar, J., Wellink, A., Richir, M.C. & van Agtmael, M.A. (2019). Digital Learning to Improve Safe and Effective Prescribing: A Systematic Review. Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics. https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.1549
title: Design prescribing DLRs with anytime-anywhere availability, manageable time demands, and directly applicable authentic content
description: From qualitative reports across included studies, the review compiles ten recommendations for future DLRs for safe and effective prescribing. The most appreciated element is availability: "By far the most appreciated feature of DLRs is the possibility to study anytime and anywhere," which promotes just-in-time learning and puts students in charge of their learning. Other recommendations include openness about required time investment with bite-size chunks, clear navigational structure for pace and revision, quizzes and game design principles, direct feedback, authentic content connected to clear learning goals, accessible and attractive design, multimedia presented in various ways, and relevant web links.
requirements: Content should have a clear connection with predefined and clearly communicated learning goals and be directly applicable
constraints: Digital communication channels such as web forums and email for peer and teacher contact remained largely unused by students
examples: The review's Table 3 lists ten elements, with anytime-anywhere availability mentioned in 13 articles and authentic, applicable content in 12 articles
key_sources: Bakkum, M.J., Tichelaar, J., Wellink, A., Richir, M.C. & van Agtmael, M.A. (2019). Digital Learning to Improve Safe and Effective Prescribing: A Systematic Review. Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics. https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.1549

article_title: Assessing the Reliability of Merging Chickering & Gamson's Seven Principles for Good Practice with Merrill's Different Levels of Instructional Strategy (DLISt7)
citation: Jabar, S. I., & Albion, P. R. (2016). Assessing the Reliability of Merging Chickering & Gamson's Seven Principles for Good Practice with Merrill's Different Levels of Instructional Strategy (DLISt7). Online Learning, 20(2). https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt1gxpcbq
title: DLISt7: A merged framework combining Chickering & Gamson's Seven Principles with Merrill's Different Levels of Instructional Strategy
description: DLISt7 is a conceptual framework that merges Chickering and Gamson's (1987) Seven Principles for Good Practice with Merrill's (2006) Different Levels of Instructional Strategy (DLIS), which describes five levels of application (Demonstration, Application, Task-centred, Activation, and Integration) charted across four levels (0-3) from "Information only" to "Task-centred integration of all three preceding levels." The 't' in DLISt7 signifies its use "as a rubric either for teaching or treatment purposes to prompt and stimulate conditional response from students." The framework was designed to function as "a set of workable principles that could guide pedagogy in a variety of contexts."
requirements: Requires a measurement instrument with clear rules of measurement, practical application, low demands on administrator and respondent, and results independent of the administrator
constraints: Validation is an unending process requiring constant re-evaluation; further replication and cross-validation by others would be valuable
target_learners: Undergraduate students in blended and online courses
target_learning_goals: Effective, efficient, and engaging online learning through structured instructional strategies
key_sources: Jabar, S. I., & Albion, P. R. (2016). Assessing the Reliability of Merging Chickering & Gamson's Seven Principles for Good Practice with Merrill's Different Levels of Instructional Strategy (DLISt7). Online Learning, 20(2). https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt1gxpcbq

article_title: Assessing the Reliability of Merging Chickering & Gamson's Seven Principles for Good Practice with Merrill's Different Levels of Instructional Strategy (DLISt7)
citation: Jabar, S. I., & Albion, P. R. (2016). Assessing the Reliability of Merging Chickering & Gamson's Seven Principles for Good Practice with Merrill's Different Levels of Instructional Strategy (DLISt7). Online Learning, 20(2). https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt1gxpcbq
title: Use DLISt7 as a rubric to assist instructional design and as a measure to evaluate effectiveness of online instruction
description: The article proposes that the validated DLISt7 instrument "can now be used as a rubric to assist the design of instruction and as a measure to evaluate the effectiveness of such instruction." It further proposes that DLISt7 be utilized "to enable the learning experienced by students to be systematically scalable to different levels of complexity," with teaching staff having flexibility in their pedagogical choices. Successively less facilitated guidance should be faded with each scaffolded task until students complete complex tasks independently.
requirements: Requires the standardized DLISt7 measurement instrument validated through factor analysis and reliability testing
constraints: Validation is unending and requires measures to be constantly evaluated and re-evaluated; further replication and cross-validation would be valuable
target_learners: Undergraduate students in blended and online courses
target_learning_goals: Effective, efficient, and engaging online learning through structured instructional strategies
key_sources: Jabar, S. I., & Albion, P. R. (2016). Assessing the Reliability of Merging Chickering & Gamson's Seven Principles for Good Practice with Merrill's Different Levels of Instructional Strategy (DLISt7). Online Learning, 20(2). https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt1gxpcbq
